paper_metadata.title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Algorithms for Loan Collection Optimization with Loan Loss Provisions

summary: The paper proposes a hybrid divide‑and‑conquer algorithm combining QAOA (T=2) on subproblems up to 35 qubits with classical reconstruction and Greedy Provision Reduction for a loan collection optimization problem with 600 borrowers and 5 actions each. Using a real Kasikornbank dataset, the hybrid approach improves expected net profit by about 70% relative to a classical baseline without QAOA while reducing provisions from ~5.4 to ~4.4 (≈18.5%). All quantum computations are performed on a classical simulator.

experiments.description: Hybrid quantum-classical loan collection optimization using divide-and-conquer, QAOA on subproblems, and classical greedy provision reduction on a real bank loan dataset.

algorithm.variant: Hybrid divide-and-conquer QAOA with state reconstruction and Greedy Provision Reduction (GPR)

hyperparameters.lambda: maximum candidates per subgraph (mentioned in pseudocode, value not specified)
hyperparameters.eta: maximum iterations in COBYLA / GPR (mentioned, value not specified)

algorithm.parameter_initialization: randomized real numbers in [0,1) for θ
classical_baselines: standalone classical GPR with random initial actions

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Each loanee is represented by M qubits; action j is encoded as qubit (i,j)=1. One action per loanee is enforced by number-preserving QAOA mixers. For the reported dataset, N=600 and M=5, so the full problem has 3000 binary decision variables, but QAOA is applied only to subgraphs of size at most ν=7 (up to 35 qubits per subproblem).
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Local constraint Σ_j x_{i,j}=1 enforced by number-preserving QAOA mixer; LLP constraint Σ_i Σ_j l_{i,j} x_{i,j} ≤ L handled classically by GPR post-processing / soft constraint

problem_instance.description: Loan collection optimization for a personal loan product from Kasikornbank with 600 loanees and 5 possible collection actions per loanee.

dataset_specification.description: 600 loanees; 5 actions per loanee; hi,j estimated from Q-learning on historical data; li,j from repayment/default, expenses, credit losses, economic conditions, interest rate and tax policy; Ai,i' from internal transactions

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Association matrix built from internal transactions; community detection via greedy modularity maximization and Louvain method; edge nodes added recursively; units made arbitrary for privacy
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Comparison of hybrid algorithm versus standalone classical GPR; results shown as functions of GPR steps k, epsilon, and number of DPO actions N_f; no independent-run count reported

hardware.framework: QAOA executed on a classical computer; specific software framework not reported

implementation_details.classical_solver: COBYLA for QAOA parameter optimization; classical greedy modularity and Louvain for partitioning; GPR for LLP reduction
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Recursive division of the financial network into subgraphs using greedy modularity and Louvain; edge-node augmentation; Q-learning-derived h_i,j
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: State reconstruction by matching edge-node assignments across subgraphs; GPR iteratively adjusts actions to reduce LLP

speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports improved expected net profit and better objective values versus a classical baseline, but does not claim or demonstrate an asymptotic quantum speedup.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require running QAOA on real hardware for many subproblems (≤35 qubits each) plus classical community detection and reconstruction; no analysis of runtime scaling or logical error-corrected resources provided.
limiting_factors: All quantum circuits executed on a classical simulator rather than QPU
QAOA applied only to small subgraphs (≤7 loanees, ≤35 qubits)
Majority of algorithmic workload handled by classical preprocessing and postprocessing
No runtime comparison with advanced classical optimization solvers
Improvement measured only in solution quality relative to a heuristic baseline (random initialization + GPR)

notes: The paper states the QAOA is performed using up to 35 qubits on a classical computer, so hardware.type is simulator_statevector / classical simulation rather than a real QPU.
No circuit depth, gate counts, shot count, or transpilation details are reported.
The paper claims improved expected net profit but does not establish an asymptotic quantum speedup; speedup_order set to none_proven.
The paper reports ~70% higher expected net profit when QAOA is included in the hybrid pipeline versus a classical GPR-only approach.
However, the quantum component is simulated and there is no demonstrated computational speedup or scaling advantage.
Therefore the result is a heuristic improvement rather than a demonstrated quantum advantage.

experiments.description: Benchmark using a simulated dataset to test generality of the hybrid divide-and-conquer QAOA + GPR algorithm.

algorithm.variant: Hybrid divide-and-conquer QAOA with state reconstruction and Greedy Provision Reduction

key_results: Synthetic dataset with N=600 loanees and M=5 actions
h_{i,j} generated using a modified Benford-like distribution
Association matrix generated from an Erdős–Rényi graph with mean degree ≈2
Hybrid algorithm consistently yields higher net profit than standalone classical GPR baseline (Appendix A, Fig. 6)
